cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-001.prompt: A sell-side analyst is invited on a site visit to a mining company she covers. The company offers to pay for her commercial flights and hotel, and scheduled commercial flights serve the site. Under Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity, what is the most appropriate action?

options.a: Accept the paid travel and disclose it in her next research report on the company
options.b: Decline the site visit so that no appearance of bias can arise
options.c: Attend, but have her firm pay for the flights and hotel rather than the issuer
options.d: Accept, because the travel is modest relative to her annual compensation

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-001.explanation: Standard I(B) guidance says that when commercial transportation is available, the analyst or her firm should pay for travel and lodging on issuer site visits; issuer-arranged transport is acceptable only when no commercial option exists. Paying her own way keeps the research value of the visit without letting the issuer buy goodwill.

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure does not cure the conflict; the guidance is to avoid issuer-paid travel when commercial options exist.
distractorExplanations.b: Declining is unnecessary: site visits are legitimate due diligence when the analyst controls the costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Materiality relative to salary is not the test; issuer-paid travel can still compromise independence.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-002.prompt: An analyst combines public industry data, her own checks with retailers, and nonmaterial comments from a company's investor-relations team. She concludes the company will miss earnings consensus and issues a sell recommendation. Under Standard II(A), which statement is most accurate?

options.a: She violated Standard II(A) because her conclusion is material and not yet public
options.b: She must hold the recommendation until the company releases its earnings
options.c: She must ask the company to disclose her conclusion before publishing it
options.d: She acted properly; her conclusion rests on a permitted mosaic of information

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-002.explanation: Under the mosaic theory, an analyst may reach a material conclusion by combining public information with nonmaterial nonpublic information. The conclusion itself is not material nonpublic information, so recommending or trading on it does not violate Standard II(A). She should keep records documenting how she reached it.

distractorExplanations.a: A material conclusion built from public and nonmaterial pieces is not MNPI; that is the point of the mosaic theory.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no waiting requirement for mosaic-based conclusions; delaying would only disadvantage her clients.
distractorExplanations.c: The analyst has no duty to have the issuer publicize her own research conclusion.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-003.prompt: A portfolio manager downgrades a widely held stock from buy to sell. Which distribution practice best meets Standard III(B) Fair Dealing?

options.a: Phone the firm's largest clients first, then email all other clients the next day
options.b: Send the change to all affected clients as close to simultaneously as possible
options.c: Notify discretionary accounts first, because the manager can trade for them immediately
options.d: Post the change on the firm's website and let clients find it when they next log in

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-003.explanation: Fair Dealing requires treating all clients fairly when disseminating recommendations or material changes to them. Firms should distribute a change to all affected clients as close to simultaneously as possible. Offering premium service levels is allowed, but never by delaying other clients' access to a changed recommendation.

distractorExplanations.a: Giving large clients a head start on a recommendation change disadvantages everyone else, which Standard III(B) prohibits.
distractorExplanations.c: Discretionary status does not justify trading those accounts ahead of other clients on a changed recommendation.
distractorExplanations.d: Passive posting does not ensure timely dissemination to affected clients, especially for a material downgrade.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-004.prompt: A 70-year-old retired client whose investment policy statement (IPS) specifies low risk tolerance and income needs places an unsolicited order to put 15% of his portfolio into a speculative biotech stock. Under Standard III(C) Suitability, what should the adviser do?

options.a: Discuss how the trade conflicts with his IPS before deciding to execute it
options.b: Execute the order without comment, because the client initiated it himself
options.c: Refuse the order, because unsolicited unsuitable trades are prohibited outright
options.d: Execute it and record the order as an update to his stated risk tolerance

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-004.explanation: For an unsolicited trade that is inconsistent with the IPS, the adviser should discuss the inconsistency with the client before executing. A small position may be executed after that discussion; if the impact on the portfolio is material, the adviser should consider updating the IPS or using a separate client-directed account.

distractorExplanations.b: Client initiation does not remove the adviser's duty to flag an unsuitable trade against the IPS.
distractorExplanations.c: The Standards do not ban unsolicited trades; they require discussion, after which the adviser may execute.
distractorExplanations.d: One order does not change a documented risk profile; an IPS update requires a genuine review with the client.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-005.prompt: Before resigning to join a competitor, an analyst emails a list of her clients' names and contact details from the firm database to her personal account. She contacts no client until after she leaves. Which statement is correct?

options.a: She violated Standard IV(A) Loyalty by taking firm records without permission
options.b: No violation occurred, because she did not solicit clients before resigning
options.c: No violation occurred, because clients she served are part of her own knowledge
options.d: A violation occurs only if she later uses the list to solicit those clients

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-005.explanation: Under Standard IV(A) Loyalty, client lists and other records are employer property. Taking them without permission is a violation even if no solicitation happens before departure. After leaving, she may contact former clients using public information or her memory, unless a non-compete agreement prevents it.

distractorExplanations.b: Not soliciting early avoids one problem, but copying firm records is a separate violation.
distractorExplanations.c: Remembering client names is acceptable; downloading the firm's database records is not.
distractorExplanations.d: The violation occurs when the firm's records are taken; later use would only compound it.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-006.prompt: A portfolio manager wants to buy shares of a stock that her firm is about to add to client accounts. Under Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, when may she buy for her personal account?

options.a: Before the client orders, if she buys fewer shares than any single client
options.b: Alongside the client orders, if she receives the same average execution price
options.c: Not while clients hold the stock, because members may not co-own client securities
options.d: After clients and the employer have had adequate opportunity to act

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-ethics-006.explanation: Standard VI(B) ranks client and employer transactions ahead of personal transactions. The manager must give client and employer trades adequate opportunity to be executed before trading for her own account. Members may own the same securities as clients, provided their personal trades never take precedence.

distractorExplanations.a: Order size is irrelevant; trading ahead of clients on a pending decision is front-running.
distractorExplanations.b: Trading alongside clients still lets her act on knowledge of pending client orders; clients must go first.
distractorExplanations.c: Members may hold the same securities as clients; they simply cannot place their trades ahead of client trades.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-006.prompt: A newly formed asset manager wants to advertise GIPS compliance for its flagship growth strategy only, while its other strategies are not prepared under GIPS. Which statement is most accurate?

options.a: It cannot: GIPS compliance is claimed firm-wide, not for one strategy
options.b: It can, provided the growth composite's results are verified by a third party
options.c: It can, because firms choose which composites they present as GIPS compliant
options.d: It cannot until the firm has built a five-year verified performance record

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-006.explanation: GIPS compliance is claimed on a firm-wide basis: all actual fee-paying discretionary portfolios must be included in at least one composite, so a firm cannot claim compliance for one strategy only. Verification is recommended but optional, and there is no minimum track record before a firm may claim compliance.

distractorExplanations.b: Verification is optional and cannot turn a partial claim of compliance into a valid one.
distractorExplanations.c: Letting firms pick which composites comply would allow cherry-picking, which GIPS is designed to prevent.
distractorExplanations.d: No minimum track record is required; firms present at least five years (or since inception) and build to ten.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.prompt: An analyst copies two paragraphs of industry analysis from a broker's research report into her own note, changing a few words and giving no attribution. Which Standard has she most likely violated?

options.a: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation
options.b: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation
options.c: Standard V(C) Record Retention
options.d: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.explanation: Presenting another analyst's work as one's own is plagiarism, which falls under Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. Light rewording does not cure it; the source must be cited. Only factual data from recognized financial and statistical reporting services may be used without acknowledgment.

distractorExplanations.a: Market manipulation involves distorting prices or trading volume, not copying another analyst's text.
distractorExplanations.c: Record retention concerns keeping records that support research, not attributing sources.
distractorExplanations.d: Confidentiality protects client information, which is not involved in this case.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-corp-finance.prompt: A candidate who has passed Level I and is registered for the next Level II exam wants to describe her status on her résumé. Which wording complies with Standard VII(B)?

options.a: Jane Doe, CFA (Level I)
options.b: Jane Doe, Level I CFA
options.c: Candidate in the CFA Program, registered for the Level II exam
options.d: Passed Level I, so on track to earn the CFA charter faster than her peers

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-corp-finance.explanation: Standard VII(B) lets a candidate state that she is a candidate in the CFA Program while registered for the next exam, and state factually which levels she has passed. There is no partial designation, so wording such as 'CFA (Level I)' is prohibited, and claims implying superior ability or a guaranteed outcome are misleading.

distractorExplanations.a: There is no partial designation; 'CFA' may not appear after a name with a level qualifier.
distractorExplanations.b: 'Level I CFA' implies a partial designation, which does not exist.
distractorExplanations.d: Stating that she passed is fine, but implying she will earn the charter faster than others overstates her ability.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-corp-finance.prompt: A charterholder works in a country whose securities law is less strict than the CFA Institute Code and Standards. She also serves clients in a second country whose law is stricter than the Code. Under Standard I(A), which rule governs her work for those clients?

options.a: The Code and Standards, because they override local securities law
options.b: Her home country's law, because that is where she is licensed
options.c: Whichever rule her employer's compliance manual chooses to adopt
options.d: The second country's law, because it is stricter than the Code

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-corp-finance.explanation: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires members to follow the stricter of applicable law or the Code and Standards. Where the clients' country imposes a stricter law than the Code, that law governs; where local law is looser than the Code, the Code governs.

distractorExplanations.a: The Code does not override stricter law; members follow whichever standard is stricter.
distractorExplanations.b: Licensing location does not set the standard; the stricter applicable rule does.
distractorExplanations.c: An employer's policy cannot lower the bar below the stricter of applicable law and the Code.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-001.prompt: An investor deposits $10,000 today in an account paying a 6% stated annual rate, compounded monthly. What is the balance after 3 years, to the nearest dollar?
cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-001.explanation: With monthly compounding, the periodic rate is 6% / 12 = 0.5% for 36 months: FV = 10,000 × 1.005^36 = $11,967. More frequent compounding raises the future value, so monthly compounding lands between annual and continuous compounding.

distractorExplanations.a: $11,800 is simple interest (6% × 3 years with no compounding).
distractorExplanations.b: $11,910 compounds annually: 10,000 × 1.06^3.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-002.prompt: A fund returns +20% in year 1 and −10% in year 2. Investors add a large amount of new money at the start of year 2. Compared with the fund's time-weighted return, its money-weighted return will most likely be:

options.a: Higher, because the new money raises the fund's ending value
options.b: Lower, because more money was invested during the weaker year
options.c: Equal, because both measures use the same two annual returns
options.d: Higher, because the money-weighted return ignores cash-flow timing

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-002.explanation: The money-weighted return is an IRR, so it weights each period by the money invested. Because most capital was in the fund during the −10% year, the MWR falls below the time-weighted return of about 3.9% a year (√(1.20 × 0.90) − 1). The TWR removes the effect of investor cash flows.

distractorExplanations.a: A larger ending value from contributions is not a return; the MWR penalizes the poor timing of the inflow.
distractorExplanations.c: The measures differ whenever cash flows occur mid-horizon; only the TWR is unaffected by them.
distractorExplanations.d: It is the time-weighted return that ignores cash-flow timing; the money-weighted return depends on it.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-003.prompt: An analyst tests the null hypothesis that a manager's mean active return is zero at a 5% significance level and rejects it. Later evidence shows the true mean active return is zero. Which error occurred, and what is its probability?

options.a: A Type II error, with probability equal to the 5% significance level
options.b: A Type I error, with probability equal to the power of the test
options.c: A Type II error, with probability equal to one minus the test's power
options.d: A Type I error, with probability equal to the 5% significance level

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-003.explanation: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error, and the significance level (α = 5%) is the probability of committing it. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null; its probability is β, and the power of the test is 1 − β.

distractorExplanations.a: A Type II error means failing to reject a false null; here a true null was rejected.
distractorExplanations.b: Power (1 − β) is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null, not of a Type I error.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the probability of a Type II error, but the error here is rejecting a true null (Type I).

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-004.prompt: Annual returns on a portfolio are normally distributed with a mean of 8% and a standard deviation of 12%. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for next year's return?
cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-004.explanation: A 95% interval for a normal distribution is the mean ± 1.96 standard deviations: 8% ± 1.96 × 12% = 8% ± 23.5%, or about −15.5% to 31.5%.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses 2.58 standard deviations, which gives the 99% interval.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses 1.645 standard deviations, which gives the 90% interval.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses ±1 standard deviation, which covers only about 68% of outcomes.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-005.prompt: A regression of a stock's monthly excess returns on the market's excess returns gives a slope of 1.25 and an R² of 0.36. Which interpretation is correct?

options.a: The market explains 36% of the variation in the stock's excess returns
options.b: The correlation between the stock's and the market's excess returns is 0.36
options.c: The stock's average excess return is 36% higher than the market's average
options.d: A 1% market excess return predicts a 0.36% excess return for the stock

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-quant-005.explanation: R² is the coefficient of determination: the share of the dependent variable's variation explained by the independent variable. In a simple regression it equals the squared correlation, so the correlation here is +0.60 (positive because the slope is positive), and a 1% market excess return predicts 1.25% for the stock.

distractorExplanations.b: R² is the correlation squared; the correlation is √0.36 = 0.60.
distractorExplanations.c: R² measures explanatory power, not a difference in average returns.
distractorExplanations.d: The predicted response comes from the slope (1.25), not from R².

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.prompt: At its current price, a firm's product has a price elasticity of demand of −0.4. If the firm raises its price by 5%, total revenue will most likely:

options.a: Fall by about 2%, because quantity demanded declines
options.b: Stay unchanged, because price and quantity changes offset
options.c: Rise by about 5%, because quantity does not react to price
options.d: Rise by about 3%, as demand at this price is inelastic

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.explanation: With elasticity of −0.4, a 5% price rise cuts quantity demanded by about 2%, so revenue changes by roughly 1.05 × 0.98 − 1 ≈ +2.9%. When demand is inelastic (|elasticity| < 1), price and total revenue move in the same direction.

distractorExplanations.a: −2% is the change in quantity, not revenue; the higher price more than offsets it.
distractorExplanations.b: Revenue is unchanged only at unit elasticity (|e| = 1).
distractorExplanations.c: Ignores that quantity demanded falls by about 2% when the price rises.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.prompt: Inflation is well above the central bank's target and unemployment is below its natural rate. Which policy mix is most consistent with bringing inflation down?

options.a: Raise the policy rate and shrink the budget deficit
options.b: Cut the policy rate and reduce the government budget deficit
options.c: Raise the policy rate and increase government deficit spending
options.d: Cut the policy rate and increase government deficit spending

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.explanation: An overheating economy calls for restrictive policy: a higher policy rate slows credit and spending, and fiscal tightening (a smaller deficit) reduces aggregate demand. Using both levers in the same restrictive direction is the most effective combination for lowering inflation.

distractorExplanations.b: A rate cut is expansionary and works against the fiscal tightening.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher deficit spending adds demand and offsets the tighter monetary policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Both levers are expansionary, which would push inflation higher.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.prompt: The USD/EUR spot rate is 1.1000 (US dollars per euro) and the JPY/USD rate is 150.00 (yen per US dollar). What is the JPY/EUR cross rate?
cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.explanation: Chain the quotes so the US dollar cancels: JPY/EUR = JPY/USD × USD/EUR = 150.00 × 1.1000 = 165.00 yen per euro.

distractorExplanations.a: 0.0061 is the inverse quote (euros per yen), not yen per euro.
distractorExplanations.b: 136.36 divides 150 by 1.10 instead of multiplying, so the dollar does not cancel.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding the two quotes has no economic meaning; cross rates come from multiplying or dividing quotes.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.prompt: In long-run equilibrium, a firm in a monopolistically competitive industry most likely:

options.a: Earns positive economic profit because product differentiation blocks entry
options.b: Earns zero economic profit while charging a price above marginal cost
options.c: Produces at minimum average total cost, as a perfectly competitive firm does
options.d: Faces a perfectly elastic demand curve at the prevailing market price

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.explanation: Low entry barriers let new rivals enter until economic profit is competed away, so long-run economic profit is zero. Because each firm's differentiated product faces a downward-sloping demand curve, it prices above marginal cost and operates with excess capacity, above minimum average total cost.

distractorExplanations.a: Differentiation gives some pricing power, but free entry erodes economic profit in the long run.
distractorExplanations.c: Downward-sloping demand means output stays below the minimum-ATC level (excess capacity).
distractorExplanations.d: Perfectly elastic demand describes perfect competition, not differentiated products.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.prompt: One worker-day produces either 1 unit of wine or 4 units of cloth in Country A, and either 1 unit of wine or 2 units of cloth in Country B. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Country A has a comparative advantage in both goods
options.b: Country A has a comparative advantage in wine
options.c: Country B has a comparative advantage in wine
options.d: Neither country gains from trade, as wine output per day is equal

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-economics-00.explanation: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost. One unit of wine costs 4 units of cloth in Country A but only 2 in Country B, so B has the comparative advantage in wine and A in cloth. Both countries gain if B exports wine and A exports cloth.

distractorExplanations.a: A country can have an absolute advantage in both goods, but never a comparative advantage in both.
distractorExplanations.b: Wine costs Country A 4 units of cloth versus 2 in Country B, so A's opportunity cost is higher.
distractorExplanations.d: Gains from trade depend on differing opportunity costs, and those differ here.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-001.prompt: Under US GAAP, how are interest paid and dividends paid classified in the statement of cash flows?

options.a: Interest paid: operating; dividends paid: financing
options.b: Interest paid: financing; dividends paid: financing
options.c: Interest paid: operating; dividends paid: operating
options.d: Interest paid: investing, as a capital cost; dividends paid: financing

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-001.explanation: US GAAP requires interest paid in operating activities and dividends paid in financing activities. IFRS is more flexible: interest paid and dividends paid may each be reported as operating or financing, which matters when comparing cash flow from operations across firms.

distractorExplanations.b: Classifying interest paid as financing is an IFRS option that US GAAP does not allow.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividends paid as operating is an IFRS option; US GAAP requires financing.
distractorExplanations.d: Interest paid is not an investing cash flow under either US GAAP or IFRS.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-002.prompt: Prices are rising and inventory quantities are stable. Compared with FIFO, a company using LIFO will most likely report:

options.a: Lower COGS, higher gross profit, and higher ending inventory
options.b: Higher COGS, lower gross profit, and lower ending inventory
options.c: Higher COGS, lower gross profit, and higher ending inventory
options.d: Higher COGS, higher net income, and lower income tax expense

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-002.explanation: LIFO charges the newest (highest) costs to COGS and leaves the oldest (lowest) costs in inventory. With rising prices that means higher COGS, lower gross profit and net income, lower taxes, and a lower balance-sheet inventory value than FIFO.

distractorExplanations.a: This describes FIFO, which leaves the newer, higher costs in inventory.
distractorExplanations.c: LIFO ending inventory holds the older, lower costs, so it is lower, not higher.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher COGS lowers net income; the lower tax comes from lower profit, not higher.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-003.prompt: A US company using LIFO reports COGS of $3,000,000. Its LIFO reserve rose from $150,000 at the start of the year to $200,000 at year-end. What would COGS have been under FIFO?
cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-003.explanation: FIFO COGS equals LIFO COGS minus the increase in the LIFO reserve: $3,000,000 − ($200,000 − $150,000) = $2,950,000. When prices rise, the reserve grows, and LIFO COGS exceeds FIFO COGS by that change.

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracts the ending reserve balance instead of the change in the reserve.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracts the beginning reserve balance instead of the change in the reserve.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the change; FIFO COGS is lower than LIFO COGS when the reserve rises.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-004.prompt: A company has a net profit margin of 8%, total asset turnover of 1.5, and a financial leverage ratio (average assets / average equity) of 2.0. What is its return on equity?
cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-004.explanation: Three-factor DuPont: ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × financial leverage = 8% × 1.5 × 2.0 = 24.0%. Each factor isolates one driver: profitability, efficiency, and leverage.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the three factors instead of multiplying them.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops at ROA (8% × 1.5) and omits the leverage factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies margin by leverage and omits asset turnover.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-005.prompt: A company spends $10 million on a long-lived asset. Compared with expensing the cost immediately, capitalizing and depreciating it will most likely produce, in the first year:

options.a: Higher net income and lower cash flow from operations
options.b: Lower net income and higher cash flow from operations
options.c: Higher net income and higher cash flow from operations
options.d: Higher net income and unchanged cash flow from operations

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-005.explanation: Capitalizing spreads the cost through depreciation, so first-year expense is lower and net income higher. The outlay is reported in investing activities instead of operating activities, so cash flow from operations is higher too, although total cash flow is the same (ignoring tax effects).

distractorExplanations.a: CFO is lower under expensing, not capitalizing, because the outlay then hits operating cash flow.
distractorExplanations.b: Only depreciation hits first-year income, so net income is higher, not lower.
distractorExplanations.d: Total cash flow is unchanged, but the outlay moves from operating to investing, so CFO rises.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-006.prompt: A company records $100,000 of straight-line depreciation in its financial statements but deducts $160,000 of accelerated depreciation on its tax return. The tax rate is 25%. What is the deferred tax effect for the year?

options.a: Deferred tax asset rises by $15,000
options.b: Deferred tax liability rises by $15,000
options.c: Deferred tax liability rises by $40,000
options.d: Deferred tax liability rises by the full $60,000

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-fra-006.explanation: Tax depreciation exceeds book depreciation by $60,000, so taxable income is lower than pretax book income and tax is deferred to later years. The deferred tax liability rises by $60,000 × 25% = $15,000.

distractorExplanations.a: Lower current taxable income defers tax to the future, which creates a liability, not an asset.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies the 25% rate to total tax depreciation instead of to the $60,000 difference.
distractorExplanations.d: $60,000 is the temporary difference; the liability is that difference times the tax rate.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-derivatives-.prompt: Under IFRS 16, a lessee signs a five-year office lease that is neither short-term nor low-value. How does the lessee report the lease?

options.a: Off balance sheet, with a straight-line rent expense in operating costs
options.b: Lease liability only, with the lease payments expensed when they are paid
options.c: Right-of-use asset and lease liability, with a single straight-line lease cost
options.d: Right-of-use asset and lease liability, with depreciation plus interest

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-derivatives-.explanation: IFRS 16 uses a single lessee model: the lessee recognizes a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, then reports depreciation on the asset and interest on the liability. US GAAP (ASC 842) also puts operating leases on the balance sheet but reports a single straight-line lease cost.

distractorExplanations.a: Off-balance-sheet rent treatment was the old IAS 17 and pre-ASC 842 operating lease model.
distractorExplanations.b: Both an asset and a liability are recognized; payments reduce the liability rather than being expensed.
distractorExplanations.c: A single straight-line lease cost is the US GAAP operating-lease presentation, not IFRS 16.
